extracted.intended_audience: business owners, industrial managers, manufacturers, and organizational leaders
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and evaluative standards for running manufacturing businesses and industrial organizations (ethics, production methods, labor policy, competition, and organizational design) as argued by Henry Ford. Emphasizes service, production, factory organization, and human factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business as a 'holy trust' that provides livelihood
rubrics_metrics.description: A great business is something sacred because it provides a livelihood for hundreds and thousands of families; the continuance of that business becomes a holy trust and is greater than the individuals who run it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance emphasizes that a business must be judged by its continued ability to provide pay envelopes; the organization is 'a going concern' whose fitness is measured by the jobs and security it supplies to families and communities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employer justified only as he can fill his job (judged solely by ability)
rubrics_metrics.description: The employer is but a man like his employees and is justified in holding his job only as he can fill it; he is to be judged solely by his ability to steer the business without endangering employee security.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/notes: the evidence of fitness is steady payrolls; an incompetent employer is 'no more fit...than would be an infant.' Emphasizes competence over title or reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmony should serve the organization's purpose, not personal harmony
rubrics_metrics.description: 'You can hardly have too much harmony in business. But you can go too far in picking men because they harmonize.' Harmony is valuable only when all members are bent on the one main purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: hiring/skinning an organization to maintain an atmosphere of feeling at the cost of thrust, counterthrust, and progress. The correct harmonizing principle is a common purpose honestly believed in and sincerely desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use 'good feeling' (likes/dislikes) as sole hiring standard
rubrics_metrics.description: When I use the term 'good feeling' I mean making one's personal likes and dislikes the sole standard of judgment. Personal like or dislike is not a valid reason against a capable man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hiring should be capability-based; 'What have your likes or dislikes to do with the facts?' — beware of favoritism and personal preference replacing objective criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of fear of the future and of veneration for the past
rubrics_metrics.description: (Creed #1) An absence of fear of the future or of veneration for the past; fearing the future limits activity and fearing failure is disgraceful. The past is useful only as it suggests progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages experimental, forward-looking action; reframes honest failure as opportunity to begin again rather than disgrace.

rubrics_metrics.name: A disregard of competition (whoever does it best should do it)
rubrics_metrics.description: (Creed #2) A disregard of competition: 'Whoever does a thing best ought to be the one to do it.' It is criminal to try to get business away from another by lowering conditions for personal gain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Context: discourages destructive tactics aimed at crowding out competitors; promotes pride in product/service and earning business by superiority rather than by coercion or undermining others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Putting service before profit
rubrics_metrics.description: (Creed #3) The putting of service before profit. Profit is a natural reward of good service but must not be the primary basis of business activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies that without profit business cannot extend; profit is inevitable when service is primary. Business justified only as it serves and gives more to the community than it takes away.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacturing is transforming materials fairly, not buying low/selling high
rubrics_metrics.description: (Creed #4) 'Manufacturing is not buying low and selling high. It is the process of buying materials fairly and, with the smallest possible addition of cost, transforming those materials into a consumable product and distributing it to the consumer.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: gambling, speculating, and sharp dealing which clog production. Emphasizes fair purchasing and minimal added cost in transformation and distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business as a profession with recognized professional ethics
rubrics_metrics.description: Business must have a professional spirit and recognized professional ethics; violating those ethics declasses a man. The professional spirit seeks integrity from pride and penalizes its own violations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: like medicine or law, business should self-detect and penalize ethical violations. A 'machine that stops' is diseased within itself — business faults are internal moral/organizational issues to be corrected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid destructive competition; favor generous rivalry
rubrics_metrics.description: Destructive competition is personal, selfish, aimed at crowding out others and monopolizing the market; it substitutes inferior products. Progress comes from a generous form of rivalry based on pride in product and desire to excel in service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes bad competition (warfare, money-motivated) from healthy rivalry (improves product/service). Destructive competition benefits no one — harms quality and collective progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversify outlets, uses, and financial enablement (avoid single-track systems)
rubrics_metrics.description: We need more diversity of outlet, use, and financial enablement; single-track systems (including money systems) are vulnerable in hard times. Example: corn stored with only two traditional outlets; find other uses (e.g., fuel alcohol) to prevent waste and market collapse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposes practical diversification (multiple channels for goods; new product uses) and structural financial protections for 'plain people' to reduce effects of economic emergencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize labor for flexibility and emergency response
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be mobile/flying squadrons of young men available for emergency conditions in harvest, mines, shops, or railroads so 'something to be done' may get done and unemployment be reduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical organizational recommendation for aligning labor supply with sudden demand; emphasizes civic and business responsibility to mobilize labor where useful work exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abolish drudgery and monotony in labor; use invention to lighten work
rubrics_metrics.description: Drudgery—not work itself—is what men object to; we must drive out the treadmill from the daily job and abolish monotony. Invention is reducing onerous tasks and should also aim to remove monotony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use machinery and management to relieve heavier burdens but also address monotony through job design and discovery of new methods; the aim is humane, dignified labor that preserves leisure earned by effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factory organization should reduce waste and mediocrity, not stifle ability
rubrics_metrics.description: Factory organization is a device to reduce waste and losses due to mediocrity and to prevent 'don't-care' individuals from doing their worst; it is not meant to hinder ambitious, clear-headed men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes that centralization moves 'brains' to mental power-plants; systems create opportunities but require able individuals. Encourages long-term patience, dependability, and allowing capable people to rise within systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advancement begins with individual development (character and skill)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every advance begins in a small way and with the individual: moving from half-interest to strength of purpose, from hesitancy to decisiveness, from apprenticeship to mastery, from dilettante to genuine joy in work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes personal virtues: persistence, responsibility, dependability. Encourages young men to accept routine, build dependability, and take a long-term view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production is the basis of abundance; scarcity results from lack of production/knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Any real scarcity of necessaries is due only to lack of production, and lack of production often stems from lack of knowledge of how and what to produce; the earth can produce enough for decent sustenance for everyone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy implication: invest in production methods, apply existing processes/pigeonholed improvements, and direct creative capacity to produce what meets real needs rather than trinkets.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Money is not wealth; money should serve higher purpose'
rubrics_metrics.description: Money itself is not wealth; it is useful only insofar as it serves to forward principles (service) and practical work. Hoarding money or simplistic redistribution are both mistaken approaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by 'two fools' — the millionaire hoarder and the penniless reformer who thinks taking money and giving it away cures ills. Emphasizes production and service as real sources of wealth rather than mere accumulation of money.
